options.why: Only a component may update its own state during render, and only under a guard.

options.why: React warns because rendering must be pure; this update belongs in an effect or handler.

explanation: Rendering must be pure. The only state update allowed during render is a component updating its own state under a condition (the "adjust state while rendering" pattern). Updating another component's state from a render produces this warning. Move the call to an event handler or an effect.

options.why: React discards each render that set its own state and immediately renders again.

options.why: React keeps re-rendering while the component keeps setting its own state.

options.text: It displays 0 first and then 1, 2 and 3 as separate commits
options.why: The intermediate renders are thrown away before anything is committed.

explanation: When a component updates its own state during render, React throws away the output and renders it again right away, before rendering children or committing. With a guard, it settles: renders at n = 0, 1, 2 set state, the render at 3 does not, and only 3 reaches the screen (four render calls, one commit). Without a guard you get "Too many re-renders". This pattern is legitimate but rare; prefer computing values during render.

options.text: It throws, because StrictMode freezes state in development
options.why: StrictMode does not freeze state; it double-invokes reducers to expose impure ones.

explanation: StrictMode calls reducers twice in development and keeps one result. A pure reducer gives the same answer both times. This one mutates `state.items`, so both calls push into the same array and the item appears twice. Returning `{ ...state }` does not help, because the nested array is still shared. Write `{ ...state, items: [...state.items, action.item] }`.
reference: react.dev: StrictMode — Fixing bugs found by double rendering

stem: An effect with an empty dependency array starts `setInterval(() => dispatch({ type: 'tick' }), 1000)`. Which statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: The count keeps increasing, because the reducer always receives the latest state
options.why: React passes current state to the reducer, so the stale closure does not matter.

options.text: `dispatch` is stable, so leaving it out of the dependency list is safe
options.why: React guarantees the same dispatch function across renders.

options.text: The count stops at 1, as with `setCount(count + 1)`
options.why: The dispatched action contains no stale value; the reducer computes from current state.

options.text: The reducer may also call `fetch` to log each tick, because it runs only once per tick
options.why: Reducers must be pure; they can run twice in StrictMode.

options.text: `dispatch` returns the new state, so the interval can read it right away
options.why: `dispatch` returns nothing; the new state shows up on the next render.

explanation: This is why `useReducer` is a classic fix for stale closures. The action only describes what happened, and React calls the reducer with the latest state when it processes the queue. Because `dispatch` never changes identity, the effect can safely have empty dependencies.

options.text: 3, because three timeouts each add one
options.why: Each timeout sets a value, but they all compute it from the same snapshot.

options.text: 1, because all three closures were created while `n` was 0
options.why: No re-render happened between the clicks, so every timeout sets 0 + 1.

options.text: 2, because the first timeout's re-render updates the later closures
options.why: Closures never update; they keep the values from the render that created them.

options.text: 0, because updates scheduled from timeouts are discarded after the handler returns
options.why: Updates from timeouts are applied normally.

explanation: The clicks do not change state, so all three handlers belong to the same render with `n` = 0. Each timeout later calls `setN(1)`. With `setN(x => x + 1)` the result would be 3, because each updater reads the pending value.

stem: If you call a state setter with a value that is `Object.is`-equal to the current state, React is guaranteed never to call your component function again because of it.

options.text: True
options.why: React may still call the component once before it can tell that nothing changed.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: React may render the component once more, but it skips its children and does not commit.

explanation: React tries to bail out early, but this "eager" check is only possible when the component has no other pending work. Otherwise React renders the component, sees the state is unchanged, and skips its children and the commit. So an unchanged setState can still log from your component body, which is one reason renders must be pure and cheap.

stem: A comment tree is stored as nested objects, `{ id, text, replies: [...] }`. Deleting a deeply nested reply is clumsy. What does normalizing the state change?

options.text: Nothing structural; React requires nested data to be deep-cloned on every update anyway
options.why: React never requires deep cloning; only the changed path needs copying.

options.text: A flat map by id with `childIds`, so a delete touches only the parent and the map
options.why: A flat structure turns a path-copying update into one or two shallow updates.

options.text: Each nested level gets its own `useState`, so updates no longer need copying
options.why: Splitting into many states across levels makes keeping them consistent harder.

options.text: The tree moves to a ref, so mutations no longer need to trigger renders
options.why: A ref would hide changes from React, so the UI would not update.

explanation: With nested state, deleting a deep node means copying every ancestor on the path. Normalized state stores entities in a flat lookup keyed by id, with relations as id arrays. Deleting a reply then means writing a new `childIds` for its parent (and optionally removing the entry from the map). This is the same idea as database normalization, and it is how Redux Toolkit's entity adapter works.

Logged after flushSync returns.

explanation: `flushSync` first runs its callback, which queues the update and logs "b". Before returning, it renders and commits that update, so "render 1" appears next. Only then does the handler continue and log "c". Without `flushSync`, the render would come after "c".

stem: State is `{ items: [i0, i1, i2] }`. An Immer-style update runs `produce(state, draft => { draft.items[0].done = true })`. Which objects in the result are new references?

options.text: Every object in the tree, because Immer deep-clones the state
options.why: Immer does not deep-clone; that would make every child look changed to React.memo.

options.text: The root, `items` and `items[0]`; the others are reused
options.why: Immer copies only the path to the change and shares everything else.

options.text: Only `items[0]`, because that is the object that was modified
options.why: Its parents must be copied too, or the root would still be the old reference.

options.text: None: Immer mutates in place
options.why: Immer records changes on a draft and returns a new state, leaving the original intact.

explanation: Immer gives you a draft, records the mutations, and builds a new state using structural sharing: every object on the path to a change is copied, and untouched subtrees keep their references. That is exactly what React needs: the root changes so state updates, and unchanged children keep their identity so memoized components can skip rendering.
Process the queue in order: 0 + 2 = 2, then 2 × 2 = 4, then "replace with 0 + 7" (the snapshot `n` is 0) = 7, then 7 − 1 = 6.
reference: react.dev: Queueing a Series of State Updates

options.text: Track the latest query in a ref and skip `setResults` when a response is for an older query
options.why: Ignoring stale responses ensures only the newest request can write state.

options.text: Abort the previous request with an `AbortController` when a new keystroke arrives
options.why: Cancelled requests never resolve with results, so they cannot overwrite newer state.

options.text: Use `setResults(prev => results)` so React applies results in order
options.why: Updaters order queued updates, not network responses that arrive out of order.

options.text: Wrap `setResults` in `flushSync` so the newest results render first
options.why: `flushSync` changes when a render happens, not which response arrives last.

options.text: Move `setQuery` after the `await` so both updates are batched together
options.why: That makes the input lag behind typing and still lets stale responses win.

explanation: Responses can arrive in any order, and each handler writes whatever it received. The fix is to make only the latest request count: compare against a "latest query" ref or request id, or abort earlier requests. If the fetch is driven by an effect instead, use an `ignore` flag set in the effect cleanup. Data libraries such as TanStack Query handle this for you.
